source_text: Igitur per haec omnia ostendit, cuius dei sapientiam loquatur inter perfectos, eius scilicet, qui sapientiam sapientium abstulerit et prudentiam prudentium inritam fecerit, qui infatuauerit sapientia mundi, stulta eligens eius et disponens in salutem. hanc dicit sapientiam in occulto fuisse, quae fuerit in stultis et in pusillis et (in) inhonestis, quae latuerit etiam sub figuris, allegoriis et aenigmatibus. reuelanda postmodum in Christo, posito in lumen nationum a creatore promittente per Esaiae uocem patefacturum se thesauros inuisibiles et occultos. nam ut absconderit aliquid is deus, qui nihil egit omnino, in quod aliquid abscondisse existimaretur, satis incredibile. ipse si esset, latere non posset, nedum aliqua eius sacramenta. creator autem tam ipse notus quam et sacramenta eius, palam scilicet decurrentia apud Israhel, sed de significantiis obumbrata, in quibus sapientia dei delitiscebat. inter perfectos narranda suo in tempore, proposita uero in proposito dei ante saecula. cuius et saecula, nisi creatoris? si enim et saecula temporibus structa sunt, tempora autem diebus et mensibus et annis compinguntur, dies porro et menses et anni solibus et lunis et sideribus creatoris signantur in hoc ab eo positis, — et erunt enim, inquit, in signa mensium et annorum — apparet et saecula creatoris esse et omne, quod ante saecula propositum dicatur, non alterius esse, quam cuius et saecula. aut probet dei sui saecula Marcion; ostendat et mundum ipsum, in quo saecula deputentur, uas quodammodo temporum, et signa aliqua uel organa eorum. si nihil demonstrat, reuertor, ut et illud dicam: cur autem ante saecula creatoris proposuit gloriam nostram? posset uideri eam ante saecula proposuisse, quam introductione saeculi reuelasset. at cum id facit paene iam totis saeculis creatoris prodactis, uane ante saecula proposuit et non magis intra saecula quod reuelaturus erat paene post saecula. non enim eius est festinasse in proponendo, cuius est retardasse in reuelando.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, through all these things, He shows whose God's wisdom He speaks among the perfect, namely, the one who has taken away the wisdom of the wise and made the prudence of the prudent foolish, who has infatuated the wisdom of the world, choosing and arranging its foolishness for salvation. He says this wisdom was in secret, which was among the foolish and the little ones and the ignoble, which was also hidden under figures, allegories, and enigmas. It was to be revealed later in Christ, who was placed as a light for the nations by the Creator, who promises through the voice of Isaiah to reveal the invisible and hidden treasures. For it is quite incredible that the God who did nothing at all would hide something, so that it would be thought that He had hidden it. If He existed, He could not be hidden, much less any of His sacraments. But the Creator is known, as are His sacraments, which are openly evident among Israel, though they are obscure in their meanings, in which the wisdom of God was delighting. These things are to be told among the perfect at their own time, having been proposed in the proposal of God before the ages. Whose ages, if not the Creator's? For if the ages are structured by times, and times are composed of days and months and years, and days and months and years are marked by the sun and moon and stars, which the Creator has placed, and it is said that they will be for signs of months and years, it appears that the ages are the Creator's and everything that is said to have been proposed before the ages belongs to no one else but the one whose ages they are. Or let Marcion prove the ages of his own God; let him show the world itself, in which the ages are appointed, as a kind of vessel of times, and some signs or instruments of them. If he does not demonstrate this, I return to say: why did the Creator propose our glory before the ages? It could seem that He proposed it before the ages, which He revealed with the introduction of the age. But since He does this when almost all the ages of the Creator have already passed, He proposed it in vain before the ages and not more within the ages what He was going to reveal almost after the ages. For it is not characteristic of the one who delayed in revealing to have hastened in proposing.

pass_b_english: All this proves whose God's wisdom Paul proclaims among the mature: the God who stripped the wise of their wisdom and frustrated the clever, who made the world's wisdom look absurd by choosing and arranging its very foolishness to save us. He declares that this wisdom lay hidden — secreted among the foolish, the lowborn, the despised — and buried beneath figures, allegories, and riddles. It was destined to be unveiled in Christ, whom the Creator set as a light for the nations, promising through Isaiah's voice to disclose invisible, hidden treasures (Isaiah). It is utterly incredible that a God who did absolutely nothing would hide something just so people would think he had hidden it. If such a god existed, he could not stay hidden, let alone his mysteries. The Creator, by contrast, is known, and so are his mysteries — displayed openly in Israel, though veiled in their meanings, where God's wisdom took its delight. These truths are to be told to the mature at the appointed time, having been purposed in God's plan before the ages. Whose ages, if not the Creator's? Since the ages are built from times, and times from days, months, and years, and those days, months, and years are marked by the sun, moon, and stars that the Creator set in place — 'they will serve as signs for seasons and for years' — the ages belong to the Creator, and whatever was purposed before the ages belongs to no one else but the One whose ages they are. Let Marcion prove his own god's ages; let him produce the world itself where those ages are reckoned, a vessel of time, and its signs and instruments. If he cannot, I press the point: why did the Creator purpose our glory before the ages? One might think he purposed it before the ages only to reveal it when the age dawned. But he does so after nearly all the Creator's ages have already run their course — so he purposed it in vain before the ages, and not so much within the ages as almost after them. For it is not the mark of the One who delayed the revealing to have rushed the purposing.

review.notes: Pass B fails on scripture citation and agency/content accuracy. 1. Scripture: Pass B includes '(Isaiah)' as an inline citation for 'promising through Isaiah's voice to disclose invisible, hidden treasures', but the Locked Latin 'per Esaiae uocem patefacturum se thesauros inuisibiles et occultos' refers to the promise made *through* the voice of Isaiah, not necessarily the content of the treasures being the quote itself; however, more critically, Pass B fails the requirement to match the citation to the actual words. The text alludes to Isaiah (likely Isaiah 45:3), but Pass B provides a bare parenthetical '(Isaiah)' which is insufficient for the 'Added identifications are REQUIRED' rule if it is meant to identify the verse, or it is a 'false citation' if it implies the quoted words are the verse. 2. Agency/Content: Pass B translates 'cuius dei sapientiam loquatur' as 'whose God's wisdom Paul proclaims'. The Locked Latin does not mention 'Paul'; it uses the third person 'loquatur' (he/she/it speaks). While Tertullian is often discussing Pauline themes, the text provided does not name Paul, and Pass A correctly avoids this addition. Pass B adds an agent ('Paul') not present in the source.
reasons: Pass B adds 'Paul' as the agent for 'loquatur' which is not in the Locked Latin: 'cuius dei sapientiam loquatur'.
Pass B uses a bare parenthetical '(Isaiah)' which fails the requirement for specific verse identification when alluding to scripture.
